claims.text: Superconductivity in refractory BCC Nb–Ta–Ti–V high-entropy alloys is governed by electron–phonon coupling.
The electron–phonon coupling governing superconductivity is sensitive to interatomic spacing.
Hydrostatic pressure modifies the alloy's lattice parameters.
Hydrostatic pressure changes the density of states at the Fermi level.
Pressure-induced changes in electronic structure tune the superconducting transition temperature.
The proposed test material is a controlled-composition, single-phase refractory BCC alloy in the Nb–Ta–Ti–V system.
Applying hydrostatic pressure up to several GPa while using in situ synchrotron XRD and superconducting measurements provides the proposed intervention.
Pressure-induced lattice and electronic-band-structure changes affect electron–phonon coupling.
Hydrostatic pressure decreases interatomic distances.
Decreasing interatomic distances alters the density of electronic states at the Fermi level.
Changes in the density of states at the Fermi level modify electron–phonon coupling strength.
Changes in electron–phonon coupling tune the superconducting gap.
Changes in electron–phonon coupling tune the superconducting transition temperature.
Increasing pressure is predicted to produce systematic shifts in transition temperature relative to the ambient-pressure baseline.
Increasing pressure is predicted to produce systematic shifts in critical magnetic field relative to the ambient-pressure baseline.
A non-flat pressure dependence in the absence of phase transitions would support electron–phonon coupling as the governing mechanism.
The hypothesis is restricted to pressures at which the alloy remains single phase without a symmetry change.
The magnitude and sign of the transition-temperature shift may depend on subtle electronic-structure parameters and experimental conditions.
No systematic change in transition temperature or critical field despite changing lattice parameters would falsify the hypothesis.
A pressure-induced phase transition would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: Pressure-induced phase transitions are defined as outside the hypothesis's valid range, but the falsification rule also treats their occurrence as falsifying the hypothesis. An out-of-bound or confounded experiment cannot simultaneously serve as a decisive falsification without further qualification.

The hypothesis says pressure will tune Tc in a predictable manner, while the uncertainty field states that even the sign of the Tc shift is unknown. The prediction is therefore only that some non-flat response will occur, not a directional prediction.
